summary: Existing RFCs let multicast traffic cross sites within one BGP/MPLS VPN. This standards-track RFC specifies procedures for an MVPN extranet, where multicast from a source in one VPN reaches receivers in another. It updates RFCs 6513, 6514 and 6625.

eli5.summary: Letting a broadcast from one private network reach receivers in another private network.

questions: what is extranet separation in mvpn
what is the extranet source extended community
how do vpns share multicast traffic
subtitle: How multicast traffic from a source in one BGP/MPLS VPN can safely reach receivers in another VPN.

tldr.problem: Multicast in BGP/MPLS VPNs only worked between sites of the same VPN, yet it is sometimes desirable for a source in one VPN to reach receivers in another, and overlapping address spaces can then deliver the wrong traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Route Targets are provisioned so that VRFs of different VPNs exchange the routes and auto-discovery routes they need, two extranet transmission models are defined for PIM or BGP as the PE-PE control plane, and receivers must discard packets that arrive on the wrong P-tunnel.
tldr.outcome: A provider can offer an extranet MVPN service under customer-set policy, at the price of strict address and Route Target rules. The RFC adds two new BGP extended communities.

facts.label: RDs for mixed-source VRF with separation

today: RFC 7900 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6513, RFC 6514 and RFC 6625. It is itself updated by RFC 8534, and no RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 let IP multicast travel from one site to another inside a single BGP/MPLS IP VPN. RFC 7900 covers the case where multicast whose source is in one VPN is received by systems in another VPN. This is called an extranet MVPN.

The RFC defines a few roles. An extranet C-source is a source allowed by policy to send to receivers in other VPNs, and an extranet C-receiver is a receiver allowed to get that traffic. Customers set the policy, and the service provider implements it by provisioning the import and export Route Targets (RTs) of the VRFs.

The customer network is assumed to run PIM-SM, in either the ASM or the SSM service model. Other customer multicast protocols, such as PIM Dense Mode, are out of scope. The provider side may use either PIM or BGP to carry customer multicast information between PEs.

The RFC advises against letting an extranet C-source also send non-extranet flows. A receiver that may get the extranet flows is not prevented from also requesting the non-extranet ones, and the provider has no control over what a source sends.
sections.eli5: Two private networks want to share some broadcasts. The customers decide who may listen, and the phone company sets up the wiring to match.

sections.title: Overlapping Address Spaces
sections.content:
Separate VPNs may reuse the same addresses, so an address can name one host in VPN-A and a different host in VPN-B. Inside one VPN that is harmless. In an extranet it is not, so the RFC adds rules. An extranet C-source address MUST be unambiguous across all the VPNs that are allowed to receive its flows, and a VRF must never be allowed to receive flows from two different sources that share an address. A multicast group address used as an extranet C-group must also be unambiguous across the VPNs involved.

Even with those rules, a single P-tunnel can still carry packets whose addresses are ambiguous for the PEs that join it. The RFC describes two cases. In the first, a P-tunnel carries both an extranet flow and a non-extranet flow. In the second, a P-tunnel carries several extranet flows whose source addresses collide. In both, a receiving VRF can end up getting the wrong flow, from the expected PE but on the wrong P-tunnel, which would corrupt the data stream.

There are two ways out. Either every receiving PE works out the expected P-tunnel for each flow and discards packets arriving on any other P-tunnel, or provisioning policies keep ambiguous flows off the same tunnel. Those policies include one C-source per (C-S,C-G) or (C-S,C-*) P-tunnel, one C-group per (C-*,C-G) P-tunnel, no P-tunnels in I-PMSI A-D routes, and no (C-*,C-*) S-PMSI A-D routes.
sections.eli5: Two clubs might both have a member called Sam. If the loudspeaker for both clubs is shared, a listener could hear the wrong Sam. So everyone must check which loudspeaker a voice came from, or the clubs must use separate loudspeakers.

sections.title: Extranet Transmission Models
sections.content:
The RFC defines two transmission models. A VRF with extranet sources or receivers must use only one, and VRFs that exchange extranet flows must use the same one.

In the single PMSI per C-flow model, a PE sends each packet of an extranet flow on only one PMSI. It has two variants. Without extranet separation, extranet and non-extranet traffic may share a P-tunnel. With extranet separation, they must never share one, which can reduce traffic delivered unnecessarily to some PEs and removes the first ambiguity above. Both variants work with PIM or BGP, except that separation is specified only for BGP.

In the multiple PMSIs per C-flow model, a PE may send the packets of an extranet flow on several PMSIs. This model is specified only for PIM, and extranet separation with it is out of scope.
sections.eli5: One way is to send each broadcast on a single channel that everyone listening tunes to. The other way is to repeat it on a different channel for each group of listeners.

sections.title: Routes and Route Targets
sections.content:
For a flow to cross VPNs, the receiving VRF must import a route that matches the source address and is eligible for UMH (Upstream Multicast Hop) selection. These routes need not be unicast routes. They MAY be SAFI 129 routes, which are used only to decide the multicast path, so receivers can get the flows without gaining unicast routes to the sources. For ASM groups the VRF must also import a route to the C-RP. Routes may be shorter than host routes, but then they can match non-extranet sources too, so the exporting VRF SHOULD avoid exporting a route that matches both kinds.

VRFs with sources and VRFs with the C-RP must also be able to unicast PIM Register and Register-Stop messages to each other, so they must import the unicast routes they need.

Route distribution is controlled by RTs. For example, source VRFs can export extranet routes with an RT such as RT-A-extranet and receiving VRFs can import it. When ambiguity is possible, RTs must be assigned so that routes for different systems with the same address share no RT. The A-D route advertising a P-tunnel must share an RT with the UMH-eligible route for the sources it carries and must share none with a route for a different source of the same address. That is how a receiver can tell that traffic is on the wrong P-tunnel.

For BGP-based inclusive tunnels, if an egress PE has n VRFs receiving a flow sent on an Ingress Replication I-PMSI, it receives n copies of the packet, one per VRF.
sections.eli5: Route Targets are like colored stickers on mail. A club only collects mail with its stickers, and the stickers are chosen so that two people with the same name never get the same sticker.

sections.title: Two New Extended Communities
sections.content:
RFC 7900 defines two Transitive Opaque Extended Communities (see RFC 4360). IANA allocated the Extranet Source Extended Community (0x04) and the Extranet Separation Extended Community (0x05).

The Extranet Source community is optional. A CE router may attach it to routes with AFI/SAFI 1/1, 1/2, 1/4, 2/1, 2/2 or 2/4 that it advertises to a PE, to mark them dynamically as extranet source routes. Its value field MUST be zero and is ignored by the PE. It is only useful when all extranet routes from a VRF carry the same set of RTs. The PE copies it onto the corresponding VPN-IP route, and route reflectors and ASBRs must not add, remove or change it. The RFC warns that a misconfigured CE could mark the wrong route and cause a VPN security violation.

The Extranet Separation community is used only when extranet separation is in use. Its value is zero on origination and ignored on reception. It is attached to UMH-eligible routes and to I-PMSI or (C-*,C-*) S-PMSI A-D routes that carry extranet traffic in that setup.
sections.eli5: These are two special stickers. One says this route is for sharing with other clubs. The other says this channel carries only shared programs.

sections.title: When PIM Carries the Control Plane
sections.content:
With PIM between PEs, each VPN has a Multidirectional Inclusive PMSI (MI-PMSI) that PIM treats like a LAN. To build an extranet, either the receiving VRFs join the source VPN's MI-PMSI or the source VRFs join the receiving VPN's MI-PMSI. The first choice supports the single PMSI model and the second supports the multiple PMSIs model.

Provisioning uses two kinds of extra RTs. A VRF with extranet sources is given an Outgoing Extranet RT and a VRF with extranet receivers is given an Incoming Extranet RT. With the single PMSI model, a receiving VRF originates an additional Intra-AS I-PMSI A-D route for each Incoming Extranet RT, each with a different RD, and PIM sees one LAN interface per MI-PMSI. A PIM Join is sent on the P-tunnel of the I-PMSI route that shares an RT with the selected UMH route, and otherwise must not be sent. Packets arriving from an unexpected incoming interface are discarded by ordinary PIM rules, which removes the ambiguities described earlier.

With the multiple PMSIs model, it is the source VRF that originates one extra I-PMSI A-D route per Outgoing Extranet RT. A packet may be replicated once for each MI-PMSI on the outgoing list, and the ambiguities do not occur because a receiving VRF only gets traffic it requested.
sections.eli5: Each club gets an outgoing sticker for what it shares and an incoming sticker for what it wants to hear. Listeners tune to every channel they have a sticker for.

sections.title: When BGP Carries the Control Plane
sections.content:
With BGP as the PE-PE control plane, only the single PMSI per C-flow model is covered. It may be used with or without extranet separation, and data may ride on inclusive tunnels only, selective tunnels only, or both.

The main rule is that the RTs on S-PMSI A-D routes and Source Active A-D routes must overlap with those of the UMH-eligible route for the same source, and every VRF that imports the UMH-eligible route must also import them. By default, such an S-PMSI route carries the same RTs as the UMH-eligible route for its source.

With extranet separation, a VRF holding both kinds of sources must have two RDs, a default RD and an extranet RD. Extranet and non-extranet traffic then use different tunnels, advertised in separate A-D routes, and the extranet routes use the extranet RD.

A receiving PE finds the expected P-tunnel by matching S-PMSI A-D routes first, then falling back to an I-PMSI A-D route. Each match requires a shared RT that is an import RT of the VRF, and when separation is used the routes must agree on the Extranet Separation community. Any packet arriving on a different P-tunnel MUST be discarded, even from the expected PE, unless all packets of both tunnels are known to come from the same ingress VRF.

When several extranet VRFs sit on one PE, that PE is a single leaf of the P-tunnel and must replicate the traffic to the VRFs. An implementation MUST support multiple extranet VRFs on a PE.
sections.eli5: When the phone company uses BGP to pass the news around, the receiver checks each broadcast against the list of channels it expected. A broadcast from the wrong channel is thrown away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6513 and RFC 6514 apply. Misconfigured RTs, as with any technology based on RFC 4364, may deliver a packet to a VPN where policy says it should not go. The RFC calls this a VPN security violation.

Several extranet-specific risks are listed. Manually configured source lists that are wrong can make traffic from a non-extranet host look like extranet traffic. An address that is ambiguous between VPNs can make a receiver get the wrong flow. A source that sends both extranet and non-extranet flows exposes the latter to extranet receivers. And a UMH-eligible route that is less specific than a host route may match non-extranet sources as well. Providers must make sure customers understand these risks, and VRFs must be able to discard traffic from the wrong P-tunnel where the ambiguity is not otherwise prevented.

The procedures do not encrypt data flows across the provider backbone, so they do not by themselves ensure privacy or integrity against attacks on that network.
sections.eli5: If the stickers are put on wrong, a broadcast can reach a club it was never meant for. The rules and checks exist so that does not happen.
